hints: Focus on the two different types of reaction here, oxidation by concentrated sulfuric acid and displacement by a more reactive halogen.
Remember that reactivity decreases down Group 17, so chlorine can displace bromine, but bromine cannot displace chlorine and iodine cannot displace bromine.
Think about which halide ion is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce sulfur in concentrated sulfuric acid to form its halogen, chloride only gives HCl while bromide gives bromine.
walkthrough:
**Recall halogen displacement rule**

A more reactive halogen will oxidise and displace a less reactive halide ion from solution. Reactivity falls down Group 17: chlorine > bromine > iodine.

$$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{Br}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^- + \text{Br}_2$$

**Recall reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid**

Concentrated sulfuric acid is an oxidising acid. Chloride ions are weak reducing agents, so they only do acid-base reaction to make HCl gas.

$$\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HCl}$$

**Compare with bromide**

Bromide ions are stronger reducing agents than chloride ions. They first make HBr, then reduce sulfur(VI) to sulfur(IV), themselves being oxidised to orange bromine vapour.

$$2\text{HBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Apply to the statements**

Sodium chloride cannot give chlorine with either concentrated sulfuric acid or bromine. Sodium bromide cannot give bromine with iodine, which is less reactive. Only sodium bromide with concentrated sulfuric acid gives bromine.

options.A: Incorrect. Concentrated sulfuric acid does not oxidise chloride ions to chlorine. Chloride is too weak a reducing agent, so only white fumes of HCl are produced by acid-base reaction.
options.B: Incorrect. This is backwards for displacement. Bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot oxidise chloride ions. The reverse reaction, chlorine displacing bromine from sodium bromide, would work.
options.C: Correct. Bromide is a stronger reducing agent than chloride. HBr formed initially is oxidised by concentrated sulfuric acid to orange bromine vapour, while the acid is reduced to sulfur dioxide.
options.D: Incorrect. Iodine is less reactive than bromine, so it cannot oxidise bromide ions to bromine. The reverse reaction, bromine displacing iodine from an iodide, would work.
